Empirical Research Plan:  “Hoy No Circula” and Air Quality & Travel Behavior in Mexico City, 1986-1993

-------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) embedded in an event-study specification.

Rationale  
• Only one city is treated, so cross-sectional controls are unavailable.  
• The policy is activated at clearly defined hours (Mon–Fri, 05:00-22:00) and not active at other hours (nights) or days (week-ends).  
• Before the policy starts, the difference between “would-be-treated” hours and “control” hours is due solely to normal diurnal/weekly patterns; after 20 Nov 1989 any additional divergence can be attributed to the driving ban.  
• Station-level hourly data allow rich fixed effects (station × hour-of-day × day-of-week) and weather controls to net out confounders and high-frequency shocks.  
• For transportation outcomes available only at lower frequency (monthly or yearly) we use an interrupted time-series/event-study model treating November 1989 as the break.

-------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
-------------------------------------------------------------
Air-pollution outcomes (hourly data)

• Treatment variable, Treat_ht:  
  1 if date ≥ 20 Nov 1989 & weekday ∈ {Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri} & hour ∈ {05,…,21}.  
  0 otherwise.

• Control group:  
  a) Within-weekday night hours (22:00-04:00) and  
  b) All week-end hours.  
These hours/days share the same geography, monitors, and contemporaneous weather but are never subject to restrictions.

• Event date: 20 Nov 1989 (midnight between Sunday and Monday).

Travel-behavior outcomes (monthly/yearly data)

• Treatment dummy equals 1 for months/years ≥ Dec 1989.

• No explicit control group, but we difference out pre-trend using city-specific linear trends; robustness: compare to a “synthetic control” built from other large Mexican states’ gasoline sales or vehicle registrations if available.

-------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of HNC, pollution levels during daytime weekday hours would have evolved in parallel to night/week-end hours, conditional on weather and fixed effects.

Plausibility: Pre-policy hourly data permit formal pre-trend tests; mobility patterns show stable day-night/week-end gaps 1986-1989.

A2. No spillovers/contamination to control hours: Drivers banned during the day do not simply shift trips wholesale into night/week-end hours in a way that changes emissions materially.

Plausibility: 22:00-04:00 is an odd window for work commuting; week-ends have different activity patterns. Some substitution is possible but unlikely to match the magnitude of lost weekday traffic.

A3. Weather exogeneity: Conditional on measured temperature, humidity, and wind, residual meteorology is uncorrelated with policy enactment.

Plausibility: Policy start date unrelated to specific daily weather; rich controls and station FE mitigate remaining concerns.

A4. Enforcement unchanged over study period conditional on “treated” hours: Police did not differentially enforce the policy at night or week-ends.

Plausibility: By design enforcement is zero outside treatment window.

-------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential seasonality (holiday effect around late November).  
 Mitigation: Remove ±14 days around implementation (“donut”); include month-of-year × day-of-week fixed effects; run placebo break in Nov 1988.

T2. Pollution transport / atmospheric inversions differ between day and night.  
 Mitigation: Control flexibly for hour-of-day × station FE and weather; report robustness restricting to adjacent hours (e.g., compare 04:00-10:00 only).

T3. Behavioral offset (fleet purchases, more taxis) raises emissions, hiding short-run gains.  
 Mitigation: Estimate policy effect in weekly windows (event study) to capture immediate vs. medium-run adaptation; use transportation datasets to document offsets.

-------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(lubridate)    # dates
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)

# --- 5.1  Load Hourly Pollution Data
poll <- fread("mexico_pollution_1986_1993.csv")  # assume wide panel
# Columns: station_id, datetime, co, no2, o3, nox, so2, temp, humid, wind

# --- 5.2  Construct Variables
poll[, date      := as.Date(datetime)]
poll[, year      := year(date)]
poll[, month     := month(date)]
poll[, dow       := wday(date, label = TRUE)]        # Sun = 1
poll[, hour      := hour(datetime)]

# Treatment period indicator
policy_start <- as.Date("1989-11-20")
poll[, post      := as.integer(date >= policy_start)]

# Hour/day windows
poll[, weekday   := dow %in% c("Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri")]
poll[, daytime   := hour %between% c(5,21)]          # 5:00-21:59
poll[, treat_ht  := post * weekday * daytime]        # DID interaction

# Weather controls (flexible)
poll[, temp2 := temp^2]; poll[, wind2 := wind^2]

# --- 5.3  Main DID Regression for Ozone
fe_formula <- o3 ~ treat_ht + temp + temp2 + humid + wind + wind2 | 
              station_id + date + hour + dow

est_o3 <- feols(fe_formula, data = poll, cluster = ~date)
summary(est_o3)

# --- 5.4  Event-Study Graph
# relative hour index (hours since policy start)
poll[, rel_hour := as.numeric(difftime(datetime, policy_start, units = "hours"))]
poll[, rel_day  := floor(rel_hour/24)]
for (k in -720:720) poll[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(rel_day==k)]  # ±2 yrs window
event_fml <- update(fe_formula, . ~ i(rel_day, weekday*daytime, ref = -1) + 
                                 temp + temp2 + humid + wind + wind2 | 
                                 station_id + dow + hour)
est_ev <- feols(event_fml, data = poll[abs(rel_day)<=365], cluster = ~date)
iplot(est_ev)  # impulse plot

# --- 5.5  Robustness: “placebo” break in 1988
poll[, post88 := as.integer(date >= as.Date("1988-11-20"))]
poll[, treat88 := post88 * weekday * daytime]
est_placebo <- feols(o3 ~ treat88 + temp + temp2 + humid + wind + wind2 | 
                     station_id + date + hour + dow,
                     data = poll[date < policy_start], cluster = ~date)
summary(est_placebo)
```
(The same loop applies to other pollutants.  For monthly time-series outcomes use `lm` with pre-trend and AR(1) errors or `fixest::feols` with Newey-West SE.)

-------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------------------
Short-run weekday daytime pollution should decrease if the ban reduces traffic. However, theory and anecdotal evidence hint at offsetting behaviors (purchase of additional cars, shift to older higher-emission vehicles, more taxis).  

Prior:  
• Ozone (secondary pollutant) – ambiguous; reduction in NOx may *increase* peak O₃ through reduced titration.  
• CO and NOx – modest decline (5-10 percent) immediately after policy.  
• Over 1–2 years, effects likely attenuate or even reverse to zero once fleet adjustments occur.  
Gasoline sales: small positive or neutral change (extra cars increase fuel use).  
Metro/bus ridership: spike of 5-8 percent in first months, decaying over time.

-------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist (Self-assessment for DID)
(C1–C5: 1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1. Parallel pre-trends verified graphically and statistically ……………………… 1  
C2. No anticipatory effects before 20 Nov 1989 ……………………………………… 1  
C3. No spillovers to control group (night/week-end) ……………………………… 0.5  
C4. Stable unit composition (monitor network unchanged) ……………………… 1  
C5. Appropriate standard-error clustering and multiple-testing discipline …… 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5  (credible but monitor spillovers carefully).

-------------------------------------------------------------
End of empirical plan
